en.title: The Book of Dao · Chapter Four · The Dao in Use
en.原文:
道沖 而用之有弗盈也 潚呵 始萬物之宗 

銼亓兌 解亓紛 和亓光 同亓塵 

湛呵 似或存 吾不知誰子也 象帝之先
en.字龕:
### 沖 *chōng* — hollow

**字 Graph** ｜ 篆 ![沖之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E6%B2%96.svg)

**文 Gloss** ｜ The *Shuowen*: 「沖，涌搖也。從水、中。讀若動。」 — "Water surging and swaying. From 水, water, and 中, the middle; read as 'move.'" But under 盅 the *Shuowen* quotes this very book: 「盅，器虛也。《老子》曰：道盅而用之。」 — "An empty vessel. Laozi says: the Dao is 盅, hollow, yet in use." The Laozi Xu Shen held in second-century hands read 盅 — the silk text's 沖 and his 盅 pass for each other, and the empty vessel is the older picture.

**像 Image** ｜ An empty cup with water swaying at its middle. What a vessel can hold it owes to its hollow — the sway you hear is the emptiness working, never able to brim over and stop.

**義 Sense** ｜ Hence "hollow," not "pouring": the Dao is the vessel that never fills, and so its use never fails. "In use it never fills" — the silk text's extra 有 makes it a law, not a luck: it is of the Dao's nature never to brim.
en.對校:
道沖而用之或不盈，淵兮似萬物之宗；挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵，湛兮似或存。吾不知誰之子，象帝之先。
:{{*| 夫執一家之量者，不能全家。執一國之量者，不能成國。窮力舉重，不能為用，故人雖知，萬物治也，治而不以二儀之道，則不能贍也。地雖形魄，不法於天則不能全其寧。天雖精象，不法於道則不能保其精。沖而用之，用乃不能窮，滿以造實，實來則溢，故沖而用之，又復不盈，其為無窮亦已極矣。形雖大，不能累其體，事雖殷，不能充其量，萬物舍此而求主，主其安在乎。不亦淵兮似萬物之宗乎。銳挫而無損，紛解而不勞，和光而不汙，其體同塵而不渝其真，不亦湛兮似或存乎。地守其形，德不能過其載，天慊其象，德不能過其覆，天地莫能及之，不亦似帝之先乎。帝，天帝也。}}
en.疏:
杳眇曰：

道經此章，言道之用也。道者萬物之所然，非以形跡可求，故首言「道沖」。沖者虛也，道以虛為體，故能容萬物而取之不竭。帛書云「道沖而用之有弗盈也」，較之王弼本「或不盈」，易「或」為「有」，其義遂密。言道之用，固有而不盈，非偶然不盈也。道至高無上，深不可測，正此虛而不竭之謂。蓋道體若虛空之器，滿以造實，實來則溢，故沖而用之，又復不盈，其為無窮亦已極矣。是以聖人法之，損之又損，以至於無為，而無不為。

「潚呵始萬物之宗」，王本作「淵兮似萬物之宗」。「潚」「淵」音近義通，皆言道體之深窪也。宗者非統治，乃本源——萬物皆自道出，故道為宗。《莊子·大宗師》云「夫道，有情有信，無為無形」，正此萬物之宗之義。

「銼亓兌，解亓紛，和亓光，同亓塵」，四事括之為一理。王弼注云「銼挫而無損，紛解而不勞，和光而不汙，其體同塵而不渝其真」，其說甚善。夫挫銳者不暴其芒，解紛者不入其爭，和光者斂華於內，同塵者混跡於眾。此道自處之方，亦聖人藏身之要也。老子以此寫道，亦以此寫聖人——道不顯露其鋒，聖人亦不以道自炫。守柔弱者，斯之謂矣。

「湛呵似或存」，王本作「湛兮似或存」。湛者浸也，深微不可測之義。「似或存」三字最妙——既非確存，亦非不存。夫道至虛而至實，非有非無，故似存而非有定在也。《易》曰「神無方而易無體」，亦可與此相發。

「吾不知誰子也」，王本作「吾不知誰之子」。句式小異，義則同也。道先天地而生，言道非後世之上帝所能比附。此句乃本章之要義所在：老子之本體論，於此明其極致——道在帝之先也。帝者，上古以天為有意志之主宰而尊之之辭；老子言道先於帝，則有意志之天亦道之所生。萬物之律，非出自上天之意，乃自然而然之理。此華夏道術不奉人格天之本根，異於他家者也。

要之，此章以虛為宗，以不盈為用，以挫銳解紛為施，以和光同塵為行，以湛若或存為體，以象帝之先為極。聖人體此，知進退存亡之道；世人溺於有為，不知虛無之妙，譬如挹水而復溢，終不能盈虛以待用也。惜夫！
en.疏英:
Yaomiao says:

This chapter of the Book of Dao speaks of the Dao in use. The Dao is that by which the ten thousand things are so — not to be sought in shapes and tracks — and so it opens with "the Dao is hollow." 沖 is emptiness: the Dao takes emptiness for its substance, and so it holds the ten thousand things and is never drawn dry. The silk text says 道沖而用之有弗盈也 — "in use it never fills" — where Wang Bi has 或不盈, "it seems not to brim": 或 exchanged for 有, and the sense tightens: that the Dao's use never brims is its nature, not its luck. The Dao is high beyond height, deep past sounding — this same inexhaustible emptiness. The Dao's substance is like an empty vessel: fill it to make solidity, and the solid comes and spills back out; hollow in use, it never brims again — inexhaustibility at its limit. So the sage patterns on it: diminish and diminish again, down to non-doing — and nothing left undone.

"Deep-sunken it seems — the ancestor where the ten thousand things begin": 潚 and Wang Bi's 淵 are near in sound and one in sense, the deep basin of the Dao's substance. Ancestor here is not ruler but root-spring: all things come out of the Dao, so the Dao is their ancestor. The Zhuangzi: "the Dao — there is feeling in it and faithfulness; no doing and no form" — the very sense of ancestor-of-the-ten-thousand-things.

"Blunts the sharp, unties the tangle, softens the shining, joins the dust" — four works, one principle. Wang Bi's note is fine: "blunted, and nothing lost; untangled, and no labor; light softened, and no stain; its body joined to dust, and its truth unchanged." Blunting the sharp is not baring one's edge; untying the tangle is not wading into the quarrel; softening the shining is gathering the blaze within; joining the dust is walking unmarked in the crowd. This is the Dao's way of holding itself — and the sage's art of hiding. Laozi writes the Dao here, and writes the sage too: the Dao does not flash its edge, and the sage does not flaunt the Dao. To keep to the soft and weak — this.

"Still and deep — seeming to be, and not to be": 湛 is immersion, deep and fine beyond sounding. The three words 似或存 are the most subtle in the chapter: not definitely there, not definitely not. The Dao is emptiest and realest — neither presence nor absence — and so it seems to be, without a fixed place of being. The Book of Changes: "the spirit has no direction; the Change has no body" — one light with this.

"I do not know whose child it is": the Dao is born before heaven and earth — meaning the Dao admits no comparison with any August Lord of later ages. This line is the chapter's peak: **the Dao is before the Lord-on-high.** 帝 is the old word for a willing, ruling Heaven; and if the Dao precedes even 帝, then the willing Heaven too is born of the Dao. The law of the ten thousand things issues from no will above — it is the self-so of things themselves. Here is the taproot of China's arts of the Dao paying homage to no personal god — and the deep parting from other houses.

In sum: emptiness for ancestor, never-brimming for use, blunting-and-untying for working, softening-and-joining for conduct, still-as-if-there for substance, before-the-August-Lord for the peak. The sage who embodies this knows the way of advance and retreat, survival and ruin. The world drowns in contrivance and knows nothing of the subtlety of the empty and absent — like ladling water until it spills: they can never stay hollow and ready for use. A pity.
en.英譯:
The Dao (道) is hollow (沖) — yet in use it never fills (有弗盈). Deep, ah (潚呵) — the ancestor from which the ten thousand things begin.

It blunts its edge, unties its tangles, softens its shining, joins its dust.

Still and deep, ah (湛呵) — as if it were there. I do not know whose child it is: it seems to come before the August Lord (象帝之先).
